title: 10 Reasons Why You Should Never, Ever Yell At Students udents/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin builds a ten-point case against yelling at students, arguing that its apparent short-term effectiveness masks serious long-term costs. His reasons span behavioral, relational, and practical territory: yelling only produces temporary compliance, doesn't actually change underlying behavior, damages student trust and willingness to cooperate, substitutes for genuine accountability, sabotages the reflective purpose of consequences like time-out, trains students to ignore a normal speaking voice, is a source of stress for the teacher, is difficult to defend to parents, looks graceless on reflection, and models poor emotional regulation to students. His prescribed alternative is building a classroom management plan that actually works and cultivating influential relationships, so that students behave because they want to rather than out of fear of an outburst.
points: Yelling produces only temporary compliance and does not change the underlying reasons for misbehavior.
Habitual yelling substitutes for genuine accountability and trains students to wait out outbursts rather than change behavior.
Yelling conditions students to ignore a normal speaking voice, requiring escalating volume over time.
Yelling is among the most common and hardest-to-defend parent complaints against teachers.
Yelling models poor emotional regulation, since students learn more from teacher behavior than teacher words.
quotes: A thorough dressing-down can stop misbehavior in its tracks. But the price is exorbitantly high.

Behavior only changes when students want to behave better–which is the result of strict accountability combined with a teacher they like and trust. In the end, yelling causes more misbehavior, not less.

Teachers who yell tend to do so instead of following their classroom management plan. Students learn quickly that if they can endure their teacher’s outburst, they can be on their way without being held accountable.
When you yell, you train your students to listen to you only when you raise your voice. In other words, they learn that unless you’re shouting, you must not really mean it.
Yelling at students is near the top of the list of parent complaints. And it's difficult to defend.
Students are more influenced by what you do than by what you say. When you yell, react emotionally to misbehavior, or otherwise lose your composure, you provide a poor model for your students.
No matter how frustrated you may get with your students, yelling should never be an option. Although it often works in the moment, the cost of gaining momentary control is much too high.
